claim: At its scheduled review of France on Friday 27 November 2026, S&P Global Ratings keeps France's long-term sovereign rating at A+ with a stable outlook.

runs.reason:
**Base rate.** In five recent S&P decisions on France that I could verify, three left both the rating and outlook unchanged: November 2024, May 2025, and May 2026. S&P shifted the outlook to negative in February 2025 and cut the rating in October 2025. That 3-of-5 record is a rough starting point, not a complete count of scheduled review dates; it excludes dates on which S&P published nothing. ([spglobal.com](https://www.spglobal.com/ratings/pt/regulatory/article/-/view/type/HTML/id/3293262?utm_source=openai))

**What moves this review.** Toward **NO**: Fitch made exactly the move that would defeat the claim on October 30, keeping France at A+ but shifting its outlook to negative. France’s economy contracted 0.1% in the third quarter, and the European Commission’s November 24 assessment put the 2027 deficit at 5.4% of GDP versus the government’s 5.0% target. The National Assembly’s first-reading rejection of the 2027 budget adds to the risk. ([zonebourse.com](https://www.zonebourse.com/actualite-bourse/fitch-maintient-la-note-de-la-france-a-a-abaisse-sa-perspective-a-negative-ce785fd8d989f320))

Toward **YES**: S&P’s October 2025 downgrade already reflected budget-consolidation risks, and it kept A+/stable in May 2026. Both houses passed the separate 2026 year-end budget bill on November 24. That does not settle the harder 2027 negotiations, but it gives S&P some reason to wait for those talks rather than revise the outlook now. ([afd.fr](https://www.afd.fr/sites/default/files/2025-11/sp-global-21-oct-2025.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**Window.** I put the chance of no S&P publication on November 27 at about 8%: the date is scheduled and AFP reported on November 25 that a release was expected. I count silence as **YES** because the specific criterion expressly includes it, despite the final sentence’s more general wording. ([aft.gouv.fr](https://www.aft.gouv.fr/en/frances-credit-ratings?utm_source=openai))

### 3. Strongest Reason the Obvious Outcome Might Fail
Considering the sharp deterioration in growth, rising borrowing costs, and Fitch's identical move from A+/Stable to A+/Negative four weeks ago, an outlook revision to negative (resolving the claim NO) is slightly more likely than an affirmation of the stable outlook. However, this outcome could fail—meaning S&P leaves the rating and stable outlook unchanged (resolving YES)—if S&P's rating committee judges that France's current fiscal and political struggles remain within the baseline tolerances already baked into the October 2025 downgrade to A+, or if the committee prefers not to act mid-way through parliament's 2027 budget deliberations and waits until the spring 2027 review. (Under the criterion, if S&P simply publishes nothing on the scheduled date, the claim resolves YES.)

runs.reason:
The unconditional base rate for a scheduled S&P sovereign review is that the agency affirms the existing rating and outlook, or publishes no formal action, in most cases. That rate falls when growth, fiscal and political indicators have clearly worsened since the prior review and a peer agency has already moved.

Dated developments since S&P’s 29 May 2026 affirmation of A+/stable point toward action. French output contracted in the first and third quarters of 2026 and is flirting with technical recession; the European Commission and IMF have cut 2026–27 growth forecasts sharply; November flash PMIs deepened the contraction and S&P Global itself flagged higher recession odds. On 30 October 2026 Fitch, citing precisely this deterioration plus higher borrowing costs, a wider deficit and political fragmentation, revised its outlook on the same A+ rating to negative. Contemporary reporting quotes economists calling a stable-to-negative outlook shift the most logical outcome for Friday’s review, while treating an outright downgrade as less likely.

The main offset is that the 2027 budget is still under parliamentary discussion, with the government seeking a compromise around a 5% deficit. Some economists therefore argue the fiscal picture remains more uncertain than decisively negative, giving S&P cover to wait rather than revise the outlook on the scheduled date.

COUNTER
The 2027 budget negotiations remain open and the government is still publicly targeting a 5% deficit, so S&P can reasonably treat the fiscal path as unresolved rather than already tilted enough to justify an outlook change. Agencies have previously declined to move France’s rating or outlook while a budget process was incomplete, and an affirmation (or silence) on Friday would be consistent with that pattern even after Fitch’s move.
